title: Marcus Aurelius and Reflective Repetition
author: James M. Lang
summary: James M. Lang opens the new academic year by defending repetition against its bad reputation among teachers and students, who associate it with mindless drilling or unhealthy rumination, arguing instead that repetition mindfully paired with reflection and experimentation is how any skill, from painting to free-throw shooting, actually develops. He illustrates the limit case with his own golf practice: hitters who blast through a full bucket of range balls without pausing to reflect get worse as fatigue sets in, while those who hit fewer balls and reflect between shots improve. He connects this to a recent rereading of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, focusing on the line 'souls are dyed by thoughts,' arguing the journal's repetitive self-exhortations model how reflective repetition can reshape a person's habitual thinking over time, akin to cognitive behavioral therapy's approach to intrusive thoughts. He closes by recommending course journals as a classroom application of the same principle, letting students document and reflect on their learning repeatedly across a semester.
points: Lang's golf-range analogy operationalizes the difference between mindless and reflective repetition: hitters who blast through a full bucket without pausing get progressively worse, while those who hit fewer balls and reflect between shots improve.

He draws directly on personal medical trauma (eleven weeks on life support, a heart transplant, and a surgery-induced stroke) to describe involuntary rumination, using it to distinguish that unhealthy repetition from the deliberate kind he's defending.

His central textual anchor is Marcus Aurelius's line 'souls are dyed by thoughts,' which he uses to argue that repeated, self-directed reflection is how the Meditations' journal format was meant to function as a self-improvement technology.

He explicitly connects Stoic self-exhortation to cognitive behavioral therapy, noting both hold that you can't simply wish away negative thoughts but can redirect them through deliberate, repeated reflective practice.
quotes: We call it "rote," which one dictionary defines as "mechanical or unthinking routine or repetition.
They would be much better served by hitting 25% of those balls and taking time to step back and think between fewer shots. The same would be true for the free throw shooter and the painter.
Your mind will take on the character of your most frequent thoughts; souls are dyed by thoughts. So dye your thoughts like these . . .
The Meditations are eminently excerptable, because while a full reading of them may yield deeper insights, most of the time Aurelius keeps telling himself the same things over and over again.

Others have pointed out the connections between Stoic philosophy and cognitive-based behavioral therapy, which likewise argues that you can't wish away your negative thoughts, but you can learn through deliberate repetition how to turn them in a different direction.

I like to think of Marcus Aurelius, sitting in a tent somewhere in Germany surrounded by hostile tribes, in the cold early morning in the 2nd century, taking just a few minutes each day to remind himself of the person he wants to be.
